lessons.title: Range, quartiles and raw-data variance
lessons.summary: Use a centre and a spread together, distinguishing the middle half from squared deviations about the mean.
lessons.objective: Use a centre and a spread together, distinguishing the middle half from squared deviations about the mean.
lessons.before: Use exact totals, order raw observations, and distinguish a frequency from a measurement. Review Measures of central tendency if you need to recover a mean or decode an origin.
lessons.ideas:
A centre alone does not describe a distribution

Two samples can have the same mean and very different variation. The range is maximum minus minimum and uses only the two extremes. The interquartile range is \(Q_3-Q_1\), measuring the span of the middle half. It is less affected by the size of an extreme value than the range.

State the raw-data quartile convention

Order every observation, including repetitions. Here, take the medians of the lower and upper halves, excluding the overall median for an odd count. This is the chapter convention, not a claim that every software package uses identical quartile positions.

Variance uses all deviations from the mean

\[\sigma^2=\frac{\sum(x-\bar{x})^2}{n}.\]\[\sigma^2=\frac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar{x}^{\,2},\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}.\]

Use divisor n for descriptive spread here. Variance has squared units; SD has the same units as the observations. A negative calculated variance signals an error or inconsistent summaries. SD is zero exactly when all observations are equal.

Changing the reference value does not erase spread

\[\begin{aligned}\sum(x-a)^2&=\sum(x-\bar{x})^2\\&\quad+n(a-\bar{x})^2.\end{aligned}\]

The square-total about a reference is smallest at the mean. A sum of squared deviations and the square of a sum are different quantities.
lessons.method:
1. Identify whether the observations are raw, grouped or coded.
  2. Recover the count, first total and square-total on one consistent scale.
  3. Find the requested spread without premature rounding.
  4. Restore all original conditions and give every valid result.
mistakes: Do not report a quartile position as a data value.
Use n, not n−1, for these descriptive summaries.
Take the non-negative square root for SD.
Equal means do not imply equal spreads.

examples.title: Same mean, different consistency
examples.question: Compare A: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and B: 0, 4, 8, 12, 16. Find their means, ranges and variances.
examples.solution:
Both means are 8. Their ranges are 8 and 16.

\[\sigma_A^2=\frac{16+4+0+4+16}{5}=8.\]\[\begin{aligned}\sigma_B^2&=\frac{64+16+0+16+64}{5}\\&=32.\end{aligned}\]

A has less variation. This is a comparison of spread, not a claim that its centre is smaller.

examples.title: Range and IQR use different parts of the data
examples.question: Find the range and IQR of 2, 3, 4, 6, 6, 7, 10, 30, using medians of halves.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\text{range}&=30-2=28,\\Q_1&=\frac{3+4}{2}=\frac72,\\Q_3&=\frac{7+10}{2}=\frac{17}{2},\\\text{IQR}&=5.\end{aligned}\]

The large final observation stretches the range; its exact size does not enter either quartile here.

examples.title: Moments recover the centred square-total
examples.question: Five observations have \(\sum x=40\), \(\sum x^2=350\). Find their mean, centred square-total and SD.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=8,\\\sum(x-8)^2&=350-5(8^2)=30,\\\sigma&=\sqrt{30/5}=\sqrt6.\end{aligned}\]

Divide the centred total by the count before taking the square root.

examples.title: The best reference for squared deviations
examples.question: For 3, 7, 9, 13, find the real a minimising \(\sum(x-a)^2\), and its minimum.
examples.solution:
The mean is 8 and the centred square-total is 52.

\[\sum(x-a)^2=52+4(a-8)^2.\]

The minimum is 52, attained only at a=8. The variance is \(52/4=13\); it is not zero.

lessons.title: Coded totals, origins and scale changes
lessons.summary: Recover original spread from coding, and handle translations, negative scales and a second reference correctly.
lessons.objective: Recover original spread from coding, and handle translations, negative scales and a second reference correctly.
lessons.before: Use exact totals, order raw observations, and distinguish a frequency from a measurement. Review Measures of central tendency if you need to recover a mean or decode an origin.
lessons.ideas:
A translation leaves spread unchanged

For \(u=x-c\),

\[\bar{x}=c+\frac{\sum u}{n}.\]\[\sigma_x^2=\frac{\sum u^2}{n}-\left(\frac{\sum u}{n}\right)^2.\]

Squaring each coded value before adding usually avoids large raw totals. Do not assume the coded mean is zero.

Decode a scale in the correct direction

If \(u=(x-a)/b\), write \(x=a+bu\), with \(b\ne0\).

\[\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=a+b\bar{u},\\\sigma_x^2&=b^2\sigma_u^2,\\\sigma_x&=|b|\sigma_u.\end{aligned}\]

A negative multiplier reverses order, but SD remains non-negative. Translations do not change range or IQR; scaling multiplies each by the absolute multiplier.

Moving from one origin to another

Write \(D_c=\sum(x-c)\), \(E_c=\sum(x-c)^2\), and \(h=d-c\). Expanding each square gives

\[\begin{aligned}D_d&=D_c-nh,\\E_d&=E_c-2hD_c+nh^2.\end{aligned}\]

The variance calculated from either pair must agree.

Recover the original totals when needed

\[\begin{aligned}\sum x&=na+b\sum u,\\\sum x^2&=na^2+2ab\sum u+b^2\sum u^2.\end{aligned}\]

Keep the cross-term: a square of a shifted variable is not just the original square plus a constant.

Finding an unknown calibration

For y=px+q with positive original SD, the new SD fixes |p|. Test both signs of p and use the mean to recover q:

\[\begin{aligned}|p|&=\sigma_y/\sigma_x,\\q&=\bar{y}-p\bar{x}.\end{aligned}\]

If the largest original reading becomes the smallest transformed reading, select p<0. If the original SD is zero, all readings coincide and this ratio cannot be used.
lessons.method:
1. Identify whether the observations are raw, grouped or coded.
  2. Recover the count, first total and square-total on one consistent scale.
  3. Find the requested spread without premature rounding.
  4. Restore all original conditions and give every valid result.
mistakes: The coded sum need not vanish.
A negative scale does not give negative SD.
Keep the cross-term when moving origins.
Decode both original totals before mixing scales.

examples.title: A convenient origin keeps the arithmetic small
examples.question: For \(u=x-100\), n=6, \(\sum u=9\), \(\sum u^2=39\). Find the original mean and SD.
examples.solution: \[\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=100+\frac96=\frac{203}{2},\\\sigma_x^2&=\frac{39}{6}-\left(\frac96\right)^2=\frac{17}{4},\\\sigma_x&=\frac{\sqrt{17}}2.\end{aligned}\]

examples.title: Undo a negative scale
examples.question: For \(u=(x-30)/(-4)\), n=8, \(\sum u=12\), \(\sum u^2=30\). Find the original mean and variance.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\bar{u}&=\frac32,\\\sigma_u^2&=\frac{30}{8}-\frac94=\frac32,\\\bar{x}&=30-4\left(\frac32\right)=24,\\\sigma_x^2&=16\left(\frac32\right)=24.\end{aligned}\]

The SD is \(2\sqrt6\), not its negative.

examples.title: Use a second origin without the raw data
examples.question: For five readings, \(\sum(x-20)=-10\), \(\sum(x-20)^2=46\). Find both totals about 25.
examples.solution:
\[\sum(x-25)=-10-25=-35.\]\[\begin{aligned}\sum(x-25)^2&=46+100+125\\&=271.\end{aligned}\]

Both origins give variance \(26/5\). The changed square-total alone does not indicate changed spread.

examples.title: Decode a square-total including its cross-term
examples.question: For \(u=(x-10)/2\), n=4, \(\sum u=6\), \(\sum u^2=14\). Find \(\sum x\), \(\sum x^2\) and the variance.

lessons.title: Reverse moments, feasible summaries and all valid branches
lessons.summary: Use variance to reconstruct missing information, retaining every feasible count or sign before applying extra conditions.
lessons.objective: Use variance to reconstruct missing information, retaining every feasible count or sign before applying extra conditions.
lessons.before: Use exact totals, order raw observations, and distinguish a frequency from a measurement. Review Measures of central tendency if you need to recover a mean or decode an origin.
lessons.ideas:
An unknown count occurs more than once

If the sum is S, square-total T and variance v, then

\[vn^2-Tn+S^2=0.\]

Solve for every positive integer count. Check n=1 separately when v is positive, because one observation cannot have positive variance. Real-valued observations do not have to be integer counts themselves.

Recovering a mean can introduce two signs

\[\bar{x}^{\,2}=\frac{T}{n}-v.\]

Both square roots may be possible. An original condition such as a positive mean can select one; do not silently add it.

Check consistency before taking a square root

\[\sum x^2\ge\frac{(\sum x)^2}{n}.\]

This follows from non-negative variance. Equality means all values equal the mean. For n≥2 real observations, this inequality is also sufficient; extra restrictions such as non-negative integers may impose more conditions.

A hidden reference must satisfy both moments

Recover c from \(\sum(x-c)=n(\bar{x}-c)\), then use the squared coded total for spread. Recheck both original equations. A quadratic candidate is a possibility to test, not an automatically valid answer.
lessons.method:
1. Identify whether the observations are raw, grouped or coded.
  2. Recover the count, first total and square-total on one consistent scale.
  3. Find the requested spread without premature rounding.
  4. Restore all original conditions and give every valid result.
mistakes: A positive quadratic root need not be an integer count.
Do not drop the negative mean without a stated condition.
A negative implied variance is not a real SD.
Keep all feasible branches before using extra information.

examples.title: Two counts can fit one pair of moments
examples.question: Real observations have \(\sum x=20\), \(\sum x^2=120\) and variance 8. Find all possible counts. Then use \(\bar{x}>3\).
examples.solution:
\[8n^2-120n+400=0.\]\[8(n-5)(n-10)=0.\]

The possibilities are n=5 and n=10, with means 4 and 2. Both moments are feasible for real observations; the extra condition selects n=5.

examples.title: A square-total does not determine the sign of the mean
examples.question: Six real observations have square-total 150 and variance 9. Find all means, then select the positive mean and its sum.
examples.solution:
\[\bar{x}^{\,2}=150/6-9=16.\]

The means are −4 and 4. The positive choice is 4, giving sum 24. It would be incomplete to give only 4 before using the extra condition.

examples.title: Recover an unrecorded origin
examples.question: Five observations have mean 12, \(\sum(x-c)=-15\), \(\sum(x-c)^2=80\). Find c and the SD.
examples.solution:
\[5(12-c)=-15\quad\Rightarrow\quad c=15.\]\[\sigma^2=80/5-(-15/5)^2=7.\]

The SD is \(\sqrt7\). The negative coded mean describes the origin, not a negative spread.

examples.title: Reject an impossible summary
examples.question: A report claims n=6, \(\sum x=30\), \(\sum x^2=140\). Explain the contradiction and find the smallest feasible square-total.
examples.solution:
\[\sigma^2=140/6-5^2=-5/3.\]

A real data set cannot have negative variance.

\[\sum x^2\ge30^2/6=150.\]

The minimum 150 is attained when all six observations equal 5.

lessons.title: Changed records and pooled variation
lessons.summary: Update complete moments when records change, and retain between-group variation when combining two samples.
lessons.objective: Update complete moments when records change, and retain between-group variation when combining two samples.
lessons.before: Use exact totals, order raw observations, and distinguish a frequency from a measurement. Review Measures of central tendency if you need to recover a mean or decode an origin.
lessons.ideas:
Replacing a record changes two totals

If a recorded value r should have been t,

\[\begin{aligned}S_{\rm new}&=S-r+t,\\T_{\rm new}&=T-r^2+t^2.\end{aligned}\]

The count is unchanged. Adding or removing a record also changes n. Adding the square of the correction is not the same as replacing the erroneous square.

Combine at most two groups through totals

\[\begin{aligned}S_i&=n_i\bar{x}_i,\\T_i&=n_i(\sigma_i^2+\bar{x}_i^{\,2}).\end{aligned}\]

Add counts, sums and square-totals, then recompute the pooled variance. First decode any incompatible origins or units.

Differences between means add spread

The pooled variance includes both within-group variance and deviations of the group means from the pooled mean. Averaging SDs ignores that second contribution. Combining observed groups differs from adding independent random variables.

Subtract a known group to recover a missing one

Subtract its count, sum and square-total from the combined values. A recovered negative variance or non-positive count is a signal to recheck the data or interpretation.

Adding a value can leave the spread unchanged

For n observations with mean μ and variance v, add one value z. Reconstructing both moments gives

\[\begin{aligned}v_{\rm new}&=\frac{n}{n+1}v\\&\quad+\frac{n}{(n+1)^2}(z-\mu)^2.\end{aligned}\]

Thus unchanged SD requires \((z-\mu)^2=(n+1)v/n\). Retain both signs when v>0; v=0 gives only z=μ.

Symmetric changes preserve the mean

Replacing μ−d and μ+d by μ−d−t and μ+d+t keeps their sum fixed. For d≥0 and t≥0 the variance becomes

\[v_{\rm new}=v+\frac{4dt+2t^2}{n}.\]

To impose an SD bound, square a non-negative bound first, solve the variance inequality, and intersect with the original t-domain.
lessons.method:
1. Identify whether the observations are raw, grouped or coded.
  2. Recover the count, first total and square-total on one consistent scale.
  3. Find the requested spread without premature rounding.
  4. Restore all original conditions and give every valid result.
mistakes: Replace r² by t², not by (t−r)².
After removal, the denominator changes as well as the totals.
Do not average group SDs.
Recover a missing group through totals, not subtraction of variances.

examples.title: Correct the observation and its square
examples.question: Five readings have sum 60 and square-total 760. One reading 8 should be 13. Find the corrected mean and SD.

examples.title: Removal changes the divisor
examples.question: Six readings have sum 48 and square-total 420. Remove one reading of 6. Find the remaining mean and variance.

examples.title: Group means contribute to pooled variation
examples.question: A has n=4, mean 8, SD 2. B has n=6, mean 13, SD 1. Find the combined mean and variance, using descriptive SDs.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}S&=32+78=110,\\T&=4(64+4)+6(169+1)\\&=1292,\\\bar{x}&=11,\\\sigma^2&=1292/10-121=41/5.\end{aligned}\]

The pooled SD is larger than either group SD because the centres differ.

examples.title: Recover the missing group
examples.question: Ten observations have mean 12 and SD 3. Four of them form group A, with mean 9 and SD 2. Find the count, mean and variance of the other group.

lessons.title: Frequency models, percentiles and multi-step spread problems
lessons.summary: Distinguish exact frequency moments, grouped estimates, interpolated percentiles and reconstructed observations.
lessons.objective: Distinguish exact frequency moments, grouped estimates, interpolated percentiles and reconstructed observations.
lessons.before: Use exact totals, order raw observations, and distinguish a frequency from a measurement. Review Measures of central tendency if you need to recover a mean or decode an origin.
lessons.ideas:
Frequencies count repetitions

\[\begin{aligned}n&=\sum f,\\\bar{x}&=\frac{\sum fx}{\sum f},\\\sigma^2&=\frac{\sum fx^2}{\sum f}-\bar{x}^{\,2}.\end{aligned}\]

Square each measurement, then weight it by frequency. Squaring the frequency-weighted value gives the wrong second moment.

Midpoints define an estimating model

For grouped data replace x by the class midpoint. Use frequencies as weights, even for unequal-width classes. Frequency density is a histogram height, not a replacement for frequency in these moment formulas. Grouped mean and SD estimate the unknown raw-data statistics.

A percentile is a value, not a cumulative count

For cumulative proportion p, locate pN and interpolate within its class, assuming uniform within-class spread:

\[\widehat{x}_p=L+\frac{pN-C}{f}\,w.\]

For the IQR find both quartiles and subtract. To find a value exceeded by k observations, use cumulative count N−k, not k.

Two missing values require independent conditions

A mean gives their sum. Variance supplies a square-total. Use both, keep the requested ordering, and substitute the recovered pair into the original totals. Complete final answers accompany, rather than replace, written reasoning.
lessons.method:
1. Identify whether the observations are raw, grouped or coded.
  2. Recover the count, first total and square-total on one consistent scale.
  3. Find the requested spread without premature rounding.
  4. Restore all original conditions and give every valid result.
mistakes: Use fx², not (fx)², for the second moment.
Weight grouped moments by frequency, not density.
Subtract measurement quartiles, not their cumulative ranks.
Recover both missing observations and retain their specified order.

examples.title: A discrete table gives exact moments
examples.question:
ValueFrequency
11
32
53

Find the mean and variance.

examples.title: Unequal widths do not change the moment weights
examples.question:
ClassFrequency
0 ≤ x < 44
4 ≤ x < 109
10 ≤ x < 205

Estimate the mean and SD using class midpoints.
examples.solution:
Use midpoints 2, 7, 15 and frequencies 4, 9, 5.

\[\begin{aligned}\sum fm&=146,\\\sum fm^2&=1582,\\\bar{x}&\approx73/9,\\\sigma&\approx\sqrt{1790}/9.\end{aligned}\]

These are exact expressions for the midpoint model, but estimates for the unknown raw observations.

examples.title: Read two quartiles and a percentile
examples.question:
BoundaryCumulative frequency
00
108
3032
5040

Assume uniform spread within each class. Estimate the IQR and the 90th percentile.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}Q_1&=10+\frac{10-8}{24}(20)=35/3,\\Q_3&=10+\frac{30-8}{24}(20)=85/3,\\\text{IQR}&=50/3,\\P_{90}&=30+\frac{36-32}{8}(20)=40.\end{aligned}\]

The cumulative targets 10, 30 and 36 are ranks, not measurement values.

examples.title: A variance supplies a second missing-value equation
examples.question: Add a<b to 2, 4, 5, 7. The six observations have mean 6 and variance 7. Find a and b.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}a+b&=36-18=18,\\a^2+b^2&=6(7+36)-94=164.\end{aligned}\]\[a^2+(18-a)^2=164.\]

The roots are 8 and 10, so \((a,b)=(8,10)\). Their order and both original moments are satisfied.

questions.prompt_html: For 1, 3, 4, 6, 6, give the exact mean, descriptive variance and SD.
questions.solution_html:
The square-total uses each individual square. Divide by the number of observations and take the non-negative root.

Complete answers

Mean: \(4\)

Descriptive variance: \(\frac{18}{5}\)

Standard deviation: \(\frac{3 \sqrt{10}}{5}\)

questions.prompt_html:
All stated summary values are exact unless described as estimates. Keep unrounded intermediate totals. Descriptive variance and SD use divisor n, not n−1. Non-exact numerical answers: 3 significant figures; exact equivalent forms are accepted.

36.9, 40.6, 39.7, 35.9, 36.4, 39.3, 36.3, 36

  1. Find \(\sum(x-40)\) and \(\sum(x-40)^2\).

    [2]

  2. Hence calculate the mean and standard deviation of the readings.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Subtract \(40\) from each reading. Square each individual deviation before adding.

\[\sum(x-40)=-18.9,\quad\sum(x-40)^2=70.01.\]

(b)

\[\bar x=40+\frac{-18.9}{8}=\frac{3011}{80},\qquad\sigma_x^2=\frac{70.01}{8}-\left(\frac{-18.9}{8}\right)^2=\frac{20287}{6400}.\]

Subtracting a constant changes the mean but not the variance. The standard deviation is \(\frac{\sqrt{20287}}{80}\).

Numerically, the standard deviation is \(1.78\) (3 significant figures).

  1. Find \(\sum(x-61)\) and \(\sum(x-61)^2\).

    [2]

  2. Hence calculate the mean and standard deviation of the readings.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Subtract \(61\) from each reading. Square each individual deviation before adding.

\[\sum(x-61)=-20,\quad\sum(x-61)^2=48.28.\]

(b)

\[\bar x=61+\frac{-20}{11}=\frac{651}{11},\qquad\sigma_x^2=\frac{48.28}{11}-\left(\frac{-20}{11}\right)^2=\frac{3277}{3025}.\]

Subtracting a constant changes the mean but not the variance. The standard deviation is \(\frac{\sqrt{3277}}{55}\).

Numerically, the standard deviation is \(1.04\) (3 significant figures).

The extra information selects the smaller mean, so \(\sum x=36(51.25)=1845\).

All stated summary values are exact unless described as estimates. Keep unrounded intermediate totals. Descriptive variance and SD use divisor n, not n−1. Non-exact numerical answers: 3 significant figures; exact equivalent forms are accepted.

Mixed-topic prerequisite: Representation of data: frequency tables.

A set of 28 observations has mean \(\frac{50}{7}\) and variance \(\frac{321}{49}\). Its frequency table is incomplete.

Value \(x\)4711
Frequency\(p\)\(q\)\(r\)

  1. Find \(\sum fx\) and \(\sum fx^2\).

    [3]

  2. Find the missing frequencies \(p,q,r\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\sum fx=28\left(\frac{50}{7}\right)=200,\quad\sum fx^2=28\left[\frac{321}{49}+\left(\frac{50}{7}\right)^2\right]=1612.\]

(b)

\[p+q+r=28,\quad 4p+7q+11r=200,\]\[16p+49q+121r=1612.\]

Use \(r=28-p-q\) to reduce to two linear equations in \(p\) and \(q\). Solving gives \(p=8,q=13,r=7\). These are non-negative integers and reproduce both moment totals.

questions.title: Equal individual spreads, unequal group means
questions.prompt_html:
All stated summary values are exact unless described as estimates. Keep unrounded intermediate totals. Descriptive variance and SD use divisor n, not n−1. Non-exact numerical answers: 3 significant figures; exact equivalent forms are accepted.

Two disjoint groups each contain 18 observations. Their means are \(35\) and \(45\), and both standard deviations are \(4\).

  1. Find the mean and standard deviation of all the observations.

    [4]

  2. Explain why the combined standard deviation is greater than \(4\), even though each group has standard deviation \(4\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

Mean \(40\); standard deviation \(6.4\).

(b)

The different group means contribute additional spread.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\bar x=\frac{18(35)+18(45)}{36}=40.\]\[\sum x^2=18\left[4^2+35^2\right]+18\left[4^2+45^2\right]=59076.\]\[\sigma^2=41,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{41}.\]

Numerically, the standard deviation is \(6.4\) (3 significant figures).

(b)

The observations vary within each group and the group means also differ. In this equal-size case the combined variance is \(4^2+\left(\frac{45-35}2\right)^2\), whose second term is positive. Averaging standard deviations would ignore it.

questions.title: Detecting an impossible summary
questions.prompt_html:
All stated summary values are exact unless described as estimates. Keep unrounded intermediate totals. Descriptive variance and SD use divisor n, not n−1. Non-exact numerical answers: 3 significant figures; exact equivalent forms are accepted.

A report gives the following totals for 20 real observations:

\[\sum x=160,\qquad\sum x^2=1265.\]

  1. Explain why these totals cannot be correct.

    [2]

  2. The count and \(\sum x\) are correct. Find the least possible corrected value of \(\sum x^2\) and describe the observations in that case.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

They would give a negative variance.

(b)

\(1280\); all 20 observations equal \(8\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\sigma^2=\frac{1265}{20}-\left(\frac{160}{20}\right)^2=- \frac{3}{4}<0.\]

A variance is an average of squared deviations and cannot be negative.

(b)

Non-negative variance requires

\[\sum x^2\geq \frac{(160)^2}{20}=1280.\]

Equality means zero variance, so every observation equals the mean \(8\).

questions.title: A summary allowing two sample sizes
questions.prompt_html:
All stated summary values are exact unless described as estimates. Keep unrounded intermediate totals. Descriptive variance and SD use divisor n, not n−1. Non-exact numerical answers: 3 significant figures; exact equivalent forms are accepted.

A set of \(n\) real observations has variance 1 and exact summaries

\[\sum(x-30)=15,\qquad\sum(x-30)^2=34.\]

  1. Find all possible values of \(n\).

    [4]

  2. Find the corresponding mean for each possible value of \(n\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[1=\frac{34}n-\left(\frac{15}n\right)^2.\]

Multiply by \(n^2\) and factorise:

\[n^2-34n+225=(n-9)(n-25)=0.\]

Both solutions are positive integers greater than one.

(b)

\[\bar x=30+\frac{15}n.\]

Substitution of each count gives the corresponding mean. Both means are consistent with the summaries; there is no further condition selecting one.
questions.hint_html: Keep n unknown in both terms of the coded variance formula.

Correct mean for the larger count, correctly paired.

A set of \(n\) real observations has variance 1 and exact summaries

  1. Find all possible values of \(n\).

    [4]

  2. Find the corresponding mean for each possible value of \(n\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:

\[1=\frac{52}n-\left(\frac{24}n\right)^2.\]

Multiply by \(n^2\) and factorise:

Both solutions are positive integers greater than one.

(b)

\[\bar x=33+\frac{24}n.\]

Substitution of each count gives the corresponding mean. Both means are consistent with the summaries; there is no further condition selecting one.

Equal non-negative standard deviations mean equal variances. Thus

\[8=\frac{64}{9}+\frac{8}{81}(z-35)^2.\]\[(z-35)^2=9=3^2.\]

Both \(z=32\) and \(z=38\) are valid.

A set of readings \(x\) has mean \(12\) and standard deviation \(3\). The readings are transformed by \(y=ax+b\), where \(a\neq0\). The transformed mean is \(40\) and the transformed standard deviation is \(7\).

  1. Find all possible pairs of values of \(a\) and \(b\).

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The mean and standard deviation transform according to

\[40=12a+b,\qquad 7=3|a|.\]

Consequently \(a=\pm \frac{7}{3}\). Substitute each sign into the mean equation to obtain \(b=12\) or \(68\), respectively.

(b)

Order is reversed only by a negative multiplier. The negative value of \(a\) must therefore be chosen.

questions.title: Changing two readings symmetrically
questions.prompt_html:
All stated summary values are exact unless described as estimates. Keep unrounded intermediate totals. Descriptive variance and SD use divisor n, not n−1. Non-exact numerical answers: 3 significant figures; exact equivalent forms are accepted.

A set of 18 real observations has mean \(40\) and variance \(25\). Two of the observations are \(36\) and \(44\). They are replaced by \(36-t\) and \(44+t\), respectively, where \(t\geq0\).

  1. Show that the mean is unchanged, and obtain an expression for the new variance in terms of \(t\).

    [4]

  2. Find the set of values of \(t\) for which the new standard deviation is at most \(\frac{\sqrt{258}}{3}\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The two old values and the two replacements both sum to \(80\), so the raw total and the mean do not change. The increase in the raw squared total is

\[(36-t)^2+(44+t)^2-(36)^2-(44)^2=16t+2t^2.\]

Divide this increase by the unchanged count \(18\). Hence

\[\sigma_{new}^2=25+\frac{16t+2t^2}{18}.\]

(b)

Squaring is valid because both standard deviations are non-negative. The condition is

\[25+\frac{16t+2t^2}{18}\leq \frac{86}{3}.\]

This simplifies to

\[t^2+8t-33\leq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(t-3)(t+11)\leq0.\]

The quadratic condition gives \(-11\leq t\leq 3\). Intersecting with \(t\geq0\) yields \(0\leq t\leq 3\). Equality at the upper boundary is included.

questions.title: Changing two readings symmetrically
questions.prompt_html:
All stated summary values are exact unless described as estimates. Keep unrounded intermediate totals. Descriptive variance and SD use divisor n, not n−1. Non-exact numerical answers: 3 significant figures; exact equivalent forms are accepted.

A set of 20 real observations has mean \(45\) and variance \(28\). Two of the observations are \(40\) and \(50\). They are replaced by \(40-t\) and \(50+t\), respectively, where \(t\geq0\).

  1. Show that the mean is unchanged, and obtain an expression for the new variance in terms of \(t\).

    [4]

  2. Find the set of values of \(t\) for which the new standard deviation is at most \(\frac{2 \sqrt{210}}{5}\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The two old values and the two replacements both sum to \(90\), so the raw total and the mean do not change. The increase in the raw squared total is

\[(40-t)^2+(50+t)^2-(40)^2-(50)^2=20t+2t^2.\]

Divide this increase by the unchanged count \(20\). Hence

\[\sigma_{new}^2=28+\frac{20t+2t^2}{20}.\]

(b)

Squaring is valid because both standard deviations are non-negative. The condition is

\[28+\frac{20t+2t^2}{20}\leq \frac{168}{5}.\]

This simplifies to

\[t^2+10t-56\leq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(t-4)(t+14)\leq0.\]

The quadratic condition gives \(-14\leq t\leq 4\). Intersecting with \(t\geq0\) yields \(0\leq t\leq 4\). Equality at the upper boundary is included.
